It changes the memory layout so that decode attention reads a list of contiguous pages via a per-request block table instead of one dense per-request cache. FLOPs are identical and total bytes are identical; what changes is coalescing efficiency and the absence of per-request reallocation copies when the sequence grows. Its real payoff is capacity (no wasted padding in the cache) and the elimination of defragmentation copies, which is a memory-capacity and CPU-overhead win rather than a bytes-per-token win. Recorded as decode_attention.
scales_with: context_length
batch_size
page size (page_block_size must be a multiple of 256 in FlashAttention's paged path, a hard kernel constraint)
num_kv_heads

flop_classes.name: Attention over the prompt (prefill / training-style causal attention)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Prefill attention AI grows linearly with sequence length, and with the GQA group ratio on top of that. Derivation for causal attention with n_q query heads, n_kv KV heads, head_dim d_h, sequence length L, bf16 KV: flops = 2*L^2*d_h*n_q (QK^T, halved by the causal mask) + 2*L^2*d_h*n_q (P*V, also halved) = 2*n_q*d_h*L^2; bytes = 2 tensors (K and V) * L*d_h*n_kv elements * 2 bytes = 4*L*d_h*n_kv. So AI = 2*n_q*d_h*L^2 / (4*L*d_h*n_kv) = (n_q/n_kv)*L/2, i.e. AI = g*L/2 flop/byte with g the GQA group ratio. The L query rows are what amortize each KV byte, and GQA multiplies the amortization because fewer K/V columns must be read per query column. Ridge crossings against the dense-bf16 balance points computed from the accelerator records (ridge = 1000*TFLOPs/GB_per_s): H100 SXM 989.5/3350 = 295.4, so L_ridge = 2*295.4/g; MI300X 1307.4/5300 = 246.7, so L_ridge = 2*246.7/g; RTX 4090 165.2/1008 = 163.9, so L_ridge = 2*163.9/g; TPU v5e 197/819 = 240.5, so L_ridge = 2*240.5/g. Numerically on H100: MHA (g=1) crosses at L = 591 tokens, GQA-4 at L = 148, GQA-8 at L = 74; on the 4090 MHA crosses at L = 328; on TPU v5e MHA at L = 481. In fp8 the ridge doubles (H100 1979/3350 = 590.7) so every L_ridge doubles as well. So prefill attention becomes compute-bound within the first few hundred tokens of essentially every model - and GQA makes it happen sooner, not later, which surprises people who read GQA as a memory optimization only. At L = 8k on H100 with GQA-4, AI = 4*8192/2 = 16,384 flop/byte, 55x the ridge: long-context prefill is a tensor-core problem, not a bandwidth problem. SEPARATE AND MORE DECISIVE NUMBER - the flop crossover, not the ridge crossing: attention flops grow as L^2 while GEMM flops grow as L, so the two trade at L* = P_layer/(n_q*d_h), which for every standard model where n_q*d_h equals hidden_size reduces to L* = P_layer/d, i.e. roughly the feed-forward expansion ratio. With geometry taken from the models' own config.json (arithmetic shown in notes): Llama-2-7B (MHA, d=4096, 11008 intermediate, 32 layers) P_layer = 202.4M and n_q*d_h = 4096, so L* = 202,375,168/4096 = 49,408 tokens; Llama-2-70B (GQA-8, d=8192, 28672 intermediate, 80 layers) P_layer = 855.6M, n_q*d_h = 8192, L* = 855,638,016/8192 = 104,448 tokens; Llama-3-8B (GQA-4, d=4096, 14336 intermediate, 32 layers) P_layer = 218.1M, L* = 218,103,808/4096 = 53,248 tokens. So attention is 1.0% of prefill flops at L=512, 4.0% at 2k, 14.2% at 8k, 39.9% at 32k and 72.6% at 128k for Llama-2-7B; for Llama-2-70B (much wider MLP per layer) the same shares are 0.5%, 1.9%, 7.3%, 23.9%, 55.7%. Note the direction of that comparison: a WIDER model defers the attention crossover further out, so a short-prompt benchmark and a 32k-prompt benchmark on different models disagree about which part is fast for reasons that are entirely in the config.
scales_with: context_length (linearly in AI, quadratically in total flops - the reason the crossover is a single computable number)
batch_size (attention for a whole batch is one big GEMM pair - AI unchanged)
num_heads and head_dim
gqa_group_ratio g = n_q/n_kv (multiplies AI directly; does NOT change attention FLOPs, only bytes)
feed_forward_width vs hidden_width (through L* = P_layer/(n_q*d_h): a model with a wide MLP per layer keeps GEMM flops dominant to a much longer context)
causal_mask (halves the flops vs a dense mask, does not change bytes)

flop_classes.name: Prefill/decode disaggregation: the KV handoff tax that separates a compute-bound phase from a memory-bound phase
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The handoff itself is AI = 0 - it is a copy, not arithmetic - so its cost is KV bytes / link bandwidth, and that ratio is the entire design constraint. Volume per request = (prompt_tokens + 1) x 2 (K and V) x num_kv_heads x head_dim x num_layers x kv_dtype_bytes, plus any MLA latent. Write it as C_bytes, and note that C_bytes is a strict lower bound on the bytes that must cross because prefill computed them and decode will read them. What makes disaggregation able to win at all is that the two phases it is separating sit at opposite points on the roofline: prefill runs a large-M GEMM (M = prompt length) so AI is high and it is compute-bound, while decode runs an M = batch GEMM so AI = batch and it is memory-bound on weights. Colocating them forces one scheduling policy and one parallelism plan onto two different bottlenecks - DistServe's stated finding is that colocating 'leads to strong prefill-decoding interferences' and 'couples the resource allocation and parallelism plans for both phases'. The payoff condition is therefore a time budget, not a FLOP budget: disaggregation wins only if the added TTFT from waiting for the handoff (C_bytes / B_link + handoff handshake latency) is smaller than the tail-ITL and interference it removes. Splitwise makes the same argument in power terms - token generation 'do[es] not require the compute capability of the latest GPUs, and can be run with lower power and cost' - and reports 1.4x throughput at 20% lower cost, or 2.35x throughput at equal cost and power.
scales_with: prompt_length (C_bytes is linear in prompt tokens - long-context requests pay the tax hardest)
num_kv_heads x head_dim x num_layers x kv_cache_dtype (the multiplicative KV volume factor; GQA and fp8 KV shrink it directly)
tensor_parallel_degree (a KV block sharded across N ranks needs N-1 extra transfers per block read on the decode side)
interconnect_bandwidth (B_link: NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node vs RDMA/InfiniBand inter-node - this is the single biggest lever)
handoff handshake round-trips (a fixed per-request latency that dominates when C_bytes is small, e.g. short prompts)
request arrival rate (concurrency on the decode pool determines whether the decode pool's fixed cost is amortised)

flop_classes.name: Multi-turn chat with prefix caching: two flop profiles from one workload (cache hit vs miss)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: A single workload with two genuinely different arithmetic-intensity profiles, and conflating them is the single most common error in prefix-cache benchmarks. MISS path = full prefill: AI = g*L/2 flop/byte for the attention term (Llama-3-8B GQA-4 at L = 2,048 gives 4*2048/2 = 4,096 flop/byte) and the whole step runs at ~124,600 flop/byte for a 32k ingest - firmly compute-bound. HIT path = the cached prefix is already in the KV cache, so the only remaining work is the GEMM for the NEW tokens plus one attention pass of t_new query rows against the whole cached sequence. For the GEMM part of the hit path, weights are still read once and now serve t_new rows instead of B rows, so AI = t_new exactly (the same identity as decode_gemm with B replaced by t_new): on Llama-2-70B, t_new = 8 gives AI = 8 flop/byte, t_new = 64 gives AI = 64. That is still memory-bound, because the model has 68.98B parameters = 136.9 GB of bf16 weights and that read is unavoidable. The decisive difference is on the ATTENTION side. On the miss path, attention flops = 2*n_q*dh*L^2 grow quadratically in the FULL prompt. On the hit path, attention flops = 2*n_q*dh*t_new*L, which is linear in L, and KV bytes read drop from O(L^2) of compute to O(L) of bytes. Concretely for Llama-2-70B at a 4,096-token cached prefix with t_new = 64: miss-path attention = 2*8192*4096^2 = 275 GFLOP; hit-path attention = 2*8192*64*4096 = 4.3 GFLOP, a 64x reduction. And the KV READS, which dominate a long-context decode step: the hit path reads the same 4096 KV positions it must, but only once per new token rather than recomputing over all 4096 rows. So the two paths sit in different regimes at the same moment: the hit path's GEMM is memory-bound at AI = t_new while its attention is far more compute-dense than a normal decode step's because it has L columns to chew on. The result is that a cache hit makes a request dramatically faster without making it compute-bound, and a cache miss makes it slower without changing its regime.
scales_with: prefix_cache_hit_rate (the dominant variable: a hit replaces a full prefill with a t_new-token forward)
t_new (new tokens after the shared prefix - sets the hit path's GEMM AI directly)
cached_prefix_length L (sets the hit path's attention work, linearly in L and in t_new)
turn_number (a k-turn conversation accumulates a prefix, so later turns hit more and ask for less)

cross_request_sharing (system prompts and few-shot blocks are shared across ALL requests, so a deployed multi-tenant service can have a high steady-state hit rate that a single-user benchmark will never show)
cache_eviction_and_compression (evicting a block converts a hit into a miss; that is the cost of memory pressure)
prefill_chunk_size (on the miss path, chunking changes the shape but not the total flops)

flop_classes.name: Prefix/radix-cache hit path: the compute-to-bandwidth inversion and the provenance requirement
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This record covers the cost-inversion and the provenance question on the hit path; the arithmetic itself (the AI = t_new GEMM identity and the 2*n_q*dh*t_new*L attention term, versus the miss path's 2*n_q*dh*L^2) is derived in [[prefix-cache-hit-miss]]. What belongs here is the shape of the trade: on a full prefix hit of length L_hit, the attention flops for those L_hit positions are not recomputed at all - they were computed once when the prefix was first seen - so what remains is the GEMM for the new tokens plus one attention pass whose queries are only the new positions. The price is paid in bytes instead of flops: the KV for L_hit tokens must be READ from wherever it lives (HBM, a DRAM tier, or a remote store), so the hit path converts a compute cost into a bandwidth cost, and the bandwidth available is set by which tier the prefix resides in rather than by kernel tiling. That inversion is the economic argument for prefix caching on shared-prefix workloads - RAG, multi-turn chat, agent loops, a fixed system prompt - and it is also why the hit path is a kv_transfer problem: a hit is a data movement that must be correct, not just fast.
scales_with: prefix_hit_length (the entire saving: attention flops avoided scale as L_hit^2)
prefix_sharing_rate across requests (a cache that nothing shares is pure overhead)
kv_residency (HBM vs DRAM vs remote determines the bytes-per-second the hit path gets)
kv_cache_layout and block_granularity (a hit must land on a block boundary or be recomputed)
block_table_and_hash_computation cost (per-request, grows with hit length)

flop_classes.name: Quantization runtime cost: dequant, scale unpacking, and batch crossover
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Quantization changes the bytes-per-flop ratio of every weight GEMM by the compression factor: a 4-bit weight format cuts weight bytes 4x versus bf16, so decode GEMM AI goes from ~B to ~4B flop/byte and the effective ridge crossing batch drops by roughly the compression factor. The overhead is that unpacking scales and converting to a compute-representable form costs real work and real memory traffic. The question that matters for serving is when quantized kernels stop paying: Marlin reports that for 4-bit weights, batches up to 16-32 still get close to the maximum ~4x quantization speedup, with batches up to 64-128 seeing gradually decreasing but still significant acceleration, and up to 2.8x end-to-end integrated with vLLM (arXiv 2408.11743). That crossover is the whole engineering question - below it, quantization is nearly free speedup; above it, the dequant traffic starts to be paid on every step.
scales_with: bits (directly sets the bytes and hence AI)
weight_group_size (smaller groups mean more scales to unpack - more overhead per element)
batch_size (THE crossover knob: AI = bits_compound_factor * B, so the batch at which dequant stops paying is set by bits)
activation_quantization_scheme (per-tensor vs per-channel dynamic quantization adds work)
hardware_native_support (emulated dequant-to-fp16 pays overhead a native path does not)

flop_classes.name: Quantized decode at high batch: where the dequantization tax comes back
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Quantization raises decode arithmetic intensity by the compression factor, which moves the roofline crossover batch DOWN by the same factor - and that is precisely why dequantization overhead reappears at high batch. For 4-bit weights, bytes fall 4x while flops are unchanged, so AI = 4*B rather than B (see decode-gemm). Against H100 SXM's dense-bf16 ridge of 295.4 flop/byte (989.5 TFLOPS / 3.35 TB/s) the ideal crossover batches are: bf16 AI = B, B_ridge = 295.4; fp8/int8 AI = 2*B, B_ridge = 147.7; 4-bit AI = 4*B, B_ridge = 73.8; 2-bit AI = 8*B, B_ridge = 36.9. The arithmetic of the crossover is not the interesting part - the interesting part is that it predicts a measurement. MARLIN reports that 'batchsizes up to 16-32 can be supported with close to maximum (4x) quantization speedup, and larger batchsizes up to 64-128 with gradually decreasing, but still significant, acceleration' (arXiv 2408.11743). The ideal 4-bit ridge of 73.8 sits INSIDE that measured 16-128 band. The roofline therefore explains why quantized decode stops paying at high batch, in the right order of magnitude, from a two-line derivation: once B exceeds ~74 on an H100, the 4-bit GEMM has enough arithmetic intensity to be compute-bound, at which point the missing 2x of peak FLOPS that bf16 has and 4-bit does not is what matters, and the dequant-to-bf16 path pays. The dequant cost itself is a fixed per-element tax that does not benefit from batching: unpacking a group's scales and converting to a compute-representable form is O(elements) work regardless of how many rows share the weights, so as B grows the useful work (2*B*P flops) grows linearly while the unpack cost (O(P) with a per-group scale load) does not - yet the total stops shrinking because the GEMM has left the memory roof. Note the term that makes it worse with batch specifically: scale unpacking. A weight group of g elements adds g scale loads per group, and with a small g (16 or 32 is common) the scale bytes are a large fraction of the weight bytes - at g = 16 and 4-bit weights, each 16-element group costs 4*16 = 64 bits of weight plus a 16-bit scale, so scales are 20% of the traffic; at g = 128 they are 2.8%. This is why weight_group_size is a serving knob and not only a quality knob.
scales_with: batch_size (THE knob: AI = bits_factor * B, so B_ridge = ridge/bits_factor - 295.4/4 = 73.8 for 4-bit on H100, and MARLIN's measured useful band of 16-128 brackets it)
bits (directly sets bytes, hence AI, hence the crossover batch: every halving of bits halves the tolerable batch)
weight_group_size g (scale bytes as a fraction of weight bytes: g=16 gives 20% overhead, g=128 gives 2.8% - a serving-relevant number that is usually quoted only as a quality knob)
activation_quantization_scheme (per-tensor dynamic quantization adds a per-token reduction and rescale; per-channel static adds nothing per token)
hardware_native_support (a native fp8/int8 tensor-core path fuses dequant into the load; an emulated dequant-to-bf16 path pays a separate pass that batching cannot amortize)
model_size (larger models have more bytes to unpack but the same ratio, so the effect is a constant factor on the step)

flop_classes.name: Logit processing and token sampling
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Also memory-bound and batch-invariant in the worst way. Reading the final logits for a vocab V from HBM costs 2*V bytes per token at bf16 (a single fp32 row is 4*V), and the softmax/top-k/renormalize arithmetic is a few multiples of V - so AI is on the order of 1-2 flop/byte and, critically, is essentially INDEPENDENT of batch: every sequence in the batch pays its own 2*V bytes even though the sampler is one kernel. The catch-all cost is the last hidden state (2*hidden_width bytes) and, on large-vocab models, the LM head weight matrix (2*hidden_width*V bytes) - the LM head is itself a GEMM over vocab-sized output and for big vocabs is a second full decode GEMM. For Llama-2-class vocab 32k and hidden 4096, the logits alone are ~256 KB per token at fp32.
scales_with: vocab_size (logit bytes per token scale linearly with V)
batch_size (logit bytes scale linearly with B - sampling gets no batching benefit per token)
num_sampled_candidates (multiple-return sampling multiplies the softmax work)
temperature_and_top_p (compute cost of the sort/partial-sort, not memory)

vocab-to-param ratio V/P (the crossover test for DEVICE-side sampling being visible at all: 2*V/P of the step's bytes = 0.0032% for Llama-3-8B, 0.00095% for a Llama-2-7B-class vocab, ~5% only for a sub-1B model with a 128k vocab)

host-vs-device placement (this decides the regime: device-side sampling is 4*V bytes/token and negligible for every modern dense model, host-side sampling moves the same 4*V bytes to the CPU plus a serialised O(n_vocab) walk and becomes a batch-driven bottleneck - see host-side-sampling-loop)
logits dtype at the sampler (vLLM casts the whole [B, V] tensor to fp32 every step regardless of the model's output dtype, doubling both the device traffic and any downstream host payload)

flop_classes.name: Sliding-window and interleaved local/global attention: local layers are O(L*w) in prefill and O(1) in cache
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: A local layer replaces the L x L causal attention matrix with L x w, so prefill flops fall by the factor L/w while bytes for K and V fall by the same factor only for the retained window - the cache per token per LOCAL layer is bounded at w and does not grow with context at all. Gemma 3 states the design directly: 'we interleave multiple local layers between each global layer, and assign a smaller span of only 1024 tokens to the local layers. Therefore, only the global layers attend to long context, and we have 1 global for every 5 local layers.' With a 5:1 local:global ratio the model-wide prefill attention cost is (5/6)*L*w + (1/6)*L*L, so at L=131072 and w=1024 the local layers contribute 0.4% of what full attention would - total prefill attention is cut ~5.9x at that length, and the cut grows linearly with L. The residual global fraction is what sets the asymptote, and this is why the ratio is the published knob: Gemma 3's ablation reports 'minimal impact on perplexity when changing this ratio' down to 7:1 local, and separately that a 7:1 local:global ratio has minimal perplexity impact. Because those global layers keep the full quadratic behaviour, hybrid-local attention changes the CONSTANT on prefill cost, never the order. Decode side, the arithmetic inverts cleanly: a local layer's decode cost is constant in context (it reads exactly w KV entries), so AI for the local part stays at ~1 flop/byte forever while the global part's bytes still grow linearly - meaning a 5:1 Gemma-3-shaped model gets ~83% of its decode attention bytes from 1/6 of its layers.
scales_with: sliding_window w (the local cost scales linearly with it)
context_length (local layers: no cache growth; global layers: linear cache, quadratic prefill)
local:global layer ratio (5:1 Gemma 3, 1:1 Gemma 2, 12:12 GPT-OSS, 1:4 Ministral-3 published pattern)
num_global_layers (the asymptotic term - irreducible without dropping global attention entirely)
batch_size (local decode AI stays at 1 flop/byte at any batch; it is a fixed cache read)

flop_classes.name: Consumer Blackwell (SM120) vs datacenter Blackwell (SM100a): one architecture name, two incompatible kernel targets
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: A pure compatibility fact with an immediate performance consequence, and the clearest example in this slice of a kernel-library support matrix changing the arithmetic. CUTLASS's README states it outright: 'The NVIDIA Blackwell SM100 architecture used in the datacenter products has a different compute capability than the one underpinning NVIDIA Blackwell GeForce RTX 50 series GPUs (SM120). As a result, kernels compiled for Blackwell SM100 architecture with arch conditional features (using sm100a) are not compatible with RTX 50 series GPUs.' The 5th-gen tensor-core PTX instructions are 'architecture-accelerated features' requiring an sm_90a or sm100a target, so a kernel using them simply does not exist for SM120 - the part falls back to the previous generation's path. Additional SM120 constraints from the ISA: sub-byte types are not supported for cp.async.bulk.tensor with direction .shared::cluster.global on sm_120a, which limits cluster-mapped FP4 pipelines specifically on consumer Blackwell. ThunderKittens lists SM120 as a settable ARCH but is 'mainly built and tested for Hopper and Blackwell' with full Blackwell support carrying MXFP8 and NVFP4 precision. FlashInfer's own support table separates SM100/SM103 (B200/B300) from SM120/SM121 (RTX 50, DGX Spark) as different rows and warns not all features are supported across all compute capabilities.
scales_with: compute capability of the target part
which kernel library and which engine
precision (sub-byte types are affected first)

flop_classes.name: Speculative decoding at scale: draft versus verify cost, and why the win shrinks as batch grows
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Both passes are memory-bound in the same way a decode GEMM is, and that is the entire reason the scheme has a ceiling. Draft: AI ~ k (reads the draft weights once for k positions). Verify: AI ~ k (reads the target weights once for k positions). A plain decode step has AI = 1. So speculative decoding raises arithmetic intensity by roughly k on both passes - it converts k sequential memory-bound steps into one memory-bound step plus k cheap ones. The batch dependence is the sharp part: a real decode step at batch B already has AI = B, so a k=4 speculative step at batch B has AI = B + k - the increment shrinks as a fraction of the total. That is why it is a latency optimization, not a throughput one: the idle bandwidth it converts does not exist once B is large. Speculative decoding is therefore a bandwidth trade, and the win is bounded by both (1 + draft_cost/target_cost) and the acceptance rate - quoting a speedup without the acceptance rate and k is an incomplete claim.
scales_with: batch_size (the dominant term: the relative benefit of raising AI from 1 to k shrinks as B grows)
draft_k (the AI increment; multiplies the k x V logit tensor and the k x L attention work)
acceptance_rate (the other half of the realised speedup)
draft_model_size (sets draft_cost/target_cost, the overhead fraction)
context_length (verify attention flops scale as k x L and become compute-relevant)

flop_classes.name: Speculative decoding: draft-model proposal pass
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The draft pass reads the draft model's weights for k tokens' worth of positions at once. With a draft of size N_d, flops = 2*k*N_d against bytes = 2*N_d (weights) + small activations, giving AI ~ k flop/byte - the batch-k of a batched decode GEMM. So the draft pass is memory-bound exactly like decode_gemm, at effective batch k; it is cheap only because N_d is a small fraction of N_target. It also runs the full KV-cache attention and norm/sample work for k positions, so its overhead is not purely the GEMMs. The design condition for the whole scheme is that the draft's per-step latency must stay below the target model's single-token latency, which is why DeepMind's speculative sampling argues parallel scoring of a short continuation costs about the same as sampling one target token (arXiv 2302.01318).
scales_with: draft_k (number of speculative positions - AI = k, and this is the entire lever)
draft_model_size (N_d relative to N_target sets the overhead fraction)
draft_depth or tree width (for tree/multi-candidate variants, which multiply draft work)
context_length (draft KV attention grows with context like any attention)

flop_classes.name: Speculative decoding: target-model verification pass
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The verify pass runs the target model over k draft positions as a batch-k forward pass. flops = 2*k*N_target, bytes = 2*N_target (weights read ONCE for all k positions) plus k times the KV-cache attention and norm work. Weights dominate: AI ~ k flop/byte. So verify is the same memory-bound regime as decode_gemm but with k instead of 1 - it is the mechanism by which speculative decoding converts k sequential memory-bound steps into one memory-bound step plus k cheap ones. Two costs are easy to forget: the attention over k queries against the full KV cache, whose flops grow as k*L (so it becomes compute-relevant for long context), and the V-wide logits for all k positions, which are k times the sampling cost and can dominate when k is large.
scales_with: draft_k (AI = k; also multiplies the logit and attention work)
context_length (verify attention flops scale as k*L and become compute-relevant)
vocab_size (k*V logits to compare)
num_accepted_tokens (realized speedup, the other half of the cost model)
logprobs request (if per-token logprobs are requested, the target logits must be preserved uncloned-and-processed, which adds a full-width copy of the k x V tensor)
draft_probs availability (ngram speculation supplies no draft_probs, saving one [num_tokens, vocab_size] tensor and one comparison pass; model speculation supplies it)

flop_classes.name: SSM / linear-RNN decode: the constant-size recurrent state update that replaces the KV cache entirely
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This class has no KV cache at all, which inverts the entire decode cost model. Per layer the state is S = d_inner * N elements (d_inner = expand*hidden, N = d_state) and each decode step does ONE state update: for Mamba-style, flops = 2*(d_inner*N*2 + d_inner*N) for the B_t@C_t product and the state write, plus the input projection; bytes = 2*d_inner*N*2 (read state, write state). So AI ~= 1 flop/byte on the state alone - it is a weight-class bandwidth cost, not an attention-class one - but the state is CONSTANT in context length, so unlike KV attention its byte count never grows. Worked example from NVIDIA Nemotron-H-8B's config.json (hidden 4096, expand 2 -> d_inner 8192, ssm_state_size 128): state = 8192*128 = 1,048,576 elements = 2.0 MiB per layer at bf16. With 48 Mamba-2 layers and 4 attention layers, resident recurrent state = 96.0 MiB per sequence, independent of context. Compare the 4 attention layers: 4*2*8*128*2 = 16,384 bytes/token = 16 KiB/token, which at 8k context is 128 MiB and already exceeds the entire recurrent state; at 128k it is 2.0 GiB. Nemotron-H states the design intent exactly: Mamba layers 'perform constant computation and require constant memory per generated token'. The corollary nobody quotes: the state is NOT free, it is a fixed per-sequence tax that stops amortising as batch grows, so at very large batch a pure-attention model with paged KV can hold more total tokens than a hybrid with 96 MiB/seq of undividable state.
scales_with: batch_size (state is per sequence, so it does NOT amortise with batch - the inverse of every other decode class)
context_length (NOT at all - this is the defining property)
ssm_state_size N
expand ratio (d_inner = expand*hidden)
num_mamba_layers (Nemotron-H-8B: 48 of 52; Granite-4.0-h-tiny: 36 of 40)
state_dtype (fp8/bf16 state is the only knob)

flop_classes.name: Why SSM and linear-RNN FLOPs do not convert into GPU FLOPs: the sequential scan bypasses the tensor cores
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The arithmetic is small and easy; the hardware is what fails. A selective-SSM step is h_t = a_t*h_{t-1} + b_t*x_t with a per-channel, input-dependent decay a_t - a rank-1-scaled recurrence whose dependence between time steps is a MULTIPLICATIVE chain. Tensor cores compute sums of independent products C = A@B within one step; they cannot express 'step t depends on the completed result of step t-1'. So the recurrence must be executed as a sequential scan over the sequence dimension, and the elements are dependent, so the parallel width over t collapses. The consequence is stated by the authors who built the fix: Transformers-are-SSMs says SSD 'thanks to its reformulation to use matrix multiplication as a subroutine, can exploit specialized matrix multiplication (matmul) units on GPUs, also known as tensor cores. As a result, it is 2-8x faster than Mamba's fused associative scan, which does not leverage matmul units.' A 2-8x gap between the fused associative scan and the matmul-reformulated version of THE SAME MATHEMATICS is the cleanest available measurement of the penalty, because nothing but the schedule changed. Corroborating measurements in the same papers: Mamba-2 SSD crosses FlashAttention-2 at sequence length 2K and is 6x faster at 16K (linear vs quadratic); Samba reports 'Mamba has significantly worse training throughput because Mamba layers have slower training speed than MLP layers' at matched scale; HGRN2's authors make the same point from the other direction, noting that in GLA/HGRN2 'each head dimension has its own decay rate, whereas in Mamba2/xLSTM/Gated Retention, all dimensions share the decay under a single head. This improves efficiency over GLA because intra-chunk computations are more amenable to tensor core-based matrix multiplication acceleration, at the cost of sacrificing the fine-grainedness of decays.' Practical AI statement: an SSM layer's theoretical flop count is a poor predictor of its wall-clock; expect realised efficiency in the range of ordinary memory-bound elementwise work, not of a GEMM, and expect the gap to be worst exactly where the model is most attractive (long sequences, where prefill dominates).
scales_with: sequence_length during prefill (the scan is O(L) but serial; the penalty is a scheduling loss, not an asymptotic one)
ssm_chunk_size (chunkwise/SSD reformulation is what buys tensor cores: 128 for Nemotron-H, 256 for Granite-4.0-h-tiny)
per-channel vs per-head decay granularity (finer decay = less tensor-core-friendly)
num_heads (the dimension that survives chunking and gets multiplied)
seq_chunk decomposition vs pure recurrence

flop_classes.name: 2:4 structured sparsity (mma.sp): halving bytes by dropping exactly half of every four
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The only mechanism in this repo that genuinely reduces work rather than reducing overhead: the tensor core skips the zero elements. From the PTX ISA, mma.sp has a dense-equivalent shape list and a sparse counterpart at doubled K - half-precision .m16n8k16 dense becomes .m16n8k32 sparse, fp8 .m16n8k32 dense becomes .m16n8k64 sparse - and the operand A is stored sparse with a metadata operand. The metadata rules are strict and are the real engineering constraint: for .f16/.bf16 at 2:4 granularity each four-element sub-chunk of a row has two zeros and two non-zeros, only the non-zeros are stored, and two 2-bit indices in the metadata record their positions; values 0b0000, 0b0101, 0b1010 and 0b1111 are INVALID and result in undefined behavior. Granularity is type-dependent and NOT uniformly 2:4 - tf32 is 1:2, and u4/s4 is pair-wise 4:8 with the zeros clustered in two-element sub-chunks. Metadata can be stored by one thread of each group of four or by a thread-pair depending on shape (the 'sparsity selector' operand), and from PTX 8.5 there are .sp::ordered_metadata variants with a restricted set of meaningful index values. wgmma has the same story at warpgroup level (mma_async.sp, sparse .f16/.bf16 at K=32 and sparse fp8 at K=64).
scales_with: sparsity pattern (only exactly-2-of-every-4 qualifies)
metadata format (plain vs ordered_metadata)
architecture generation (mma.sp, wgmma.mma_async.sp, and sparse tcgen05 kinds)

flop_classes.name: Tensor-core instruction generations: wmma/mma (Ampere) -> wgmma (Hopper) -> tcgen05 (Blackwell)
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: This is the layer that determines what a kernel can possibly do. Three generations exist and they change how a kernel must be STRUCTURED, not just how fast it runs. (1) Ampere and earlier: warp-level wmma (implicit load/store of fragments, the compiler handles element distribution) and mma (explicit fragment layout, the programmer handles it). Both are warp-synchronous - the whole warp participates, the accumulators live in registers, and the instruction blocks until it is issued in the warp's own issue stream. (2) Hopper: wgmma, issued by a warpgroup of four contiguous warps (the first warp's warp-rank must be a multiple of 4). It is ASYNCHRONOUS and runs in a separate async proxy, so it needs wgmma.fence, fence.proxy.async, commit_group and wait_group to be correct; M is always 64 (shapes are .m64nNk16 for f16/bf16/tf32 and .m64nNk32 for fp8 and int8), the accumulator can be in registers or shared memory, and sparse variants exist. The payoff is concrete: per the FA-3 author blog, without wgmma the older mma.sync reaches only about two thirds of Hopper tensor-core peak. (3) Blackwell: tcgen05, where the MMA is launched by a SINGLE THREAD rather than a warp or warpgroup, accumulates in dedicated on-chip Tensor Memory instead of registers, and can be issued across TWO CTAs in a cluster. TMEM is a 2D array - on sm_100a/sm_100f, 512 columns x 128 lanes per CTA with 32-bit cells - dynamically allocated by a single warp in units of 32 columns with power-of-2 counts, and everything allocated must be deallocated before the kernel exits. The largest single-CTA BF16/FP16 UMMA tile is 128x256x16, about twice the largest Hopper WGMMA atom, and 2-CTA mode reaches 256x256x16.
scales_with: architecture generation
CTA group size (1 or 2 for tcgen05)
accumulator location (registers vs TMEM), which determines how many pipeline stages fit before spilling
precision (fp8 and fp4 paths have their own kinds and larger MMA_K)

flop_classes.name: Tensor Memory (TMEM): a third accumulator store, between registers and shared memory
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: TMEM changes the capacity budget of a GEMM or attention mainloop rather than the roofline. It is a dedicated on-chip scratchpad wired into the tensor cores, with structure and rules that come straight from the PTX ISA: on sm_100a/sm_100f it is a two-dimensional matrix of 512 columns and 128 lanes per CTA with 32-bit cells, addressed by a 32-bit value whose high 16 bits are the lane and low 16 bits the column; allocation is dynamic, performed by a SINGLE WARP in the CTA, in units of 32 columns with a power-of-2 column count, and every allocation must be deallocated before the kernel exits. The arithmetic consequence is about pipelining depth rather than bytes: because MMA accumulators and operands can live in TMEM instead of registers, a kernel can keep several MMAs in flight and run elementwise work on the CUDA cores concurrently. FA-4's backward pass is the concrete example - it stores S and P in TMEM in stages (S and P share one column set, dP/dS/dQ share another, because five full accumulators do not fit), stores transposed intermediates directly in TMEM in the exact operand-A layout the dV and dK MMAs consume (removing a shared-memory round trip), and notes tcgen05.mma can source operand A from TMEM.
scales_with: TMEM column budget per CTA (512 on sm_100a, extended to 576 per CUTLASS's Blackwell/Rubin entries)
number of MMAs kept in flight
CTA group size (2-CTA MMA spans both CTAs' TMEM)

flop_classes.name: Multi-GPU tensor-parallel inference: the per-layer all-reduce and the batch at which it matters
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: Pure data movement, AI = 0 - like kv_transfer, this class performs no arithmetic, so every question about it is a bandwidth question. Tensor parallelism shards each layer's weight matrices across N devices and inserts two communication ops per layer; Megatron-LM's contribution is exactly this placement, described as implementable 'with the insertion of a few communication operations' (arXiv 1909.08053). The op that matters in inference is the all-reduce over the hidden dimension, because row-parallel projections leave a partial sum on every rank that must be summed. Payload: with batch B and hidden width d in bf16, each rank contributes B*d*2 bytes; a ring all-reduce moves 2*(N-1)/N * 2*s bytes per rank, which for N >= 4 rounds to 4*s, i.e. 4*B*d bytes per rank per layer. Crossover: set the all-reduce time equal to the weight-read time it competes with. 4*B*d/BW_link = 2*P_layer/BW_hbm  =>  B* = P_layer*BW_link / (2*d*BW_hbm). For Llama-2-7B geometry (d = 4096, 11008 intermediate, 32 layers; P_layer = 4096*4096 + 2*4096*4096 + 4096*4096 + 3*4096*11008 = 202,375,168) on an H100 SXM (BW_hbm = 3350 GB/s): B* = 202,375,168 * BW_link / (2 * 4096 * 3350). With NVLink 4 at the full per-GPU per-direction 450 GB/s (18 links x 25 GB/s), B* = 202,375,168*450/(2*4096*3350) = 3,318 - far above any real serving batch, so the all-reduce is irrelevant. With a single NVLink 4 link at 25 GB/s per direction, B* = 184. On PCIe 4.0 x16 at 31.5 GB/s per direction, B* = 232. On PCIe 5.0 x16 at 63 GB/s, B* = 465. On an AMD Infinity Fabric link at 64 GB/s, B* = 472; on xGMI at 50 GB/s, B* = 369. So the same model on the same HBM sees its tensor-parallel crossover batch move by a factor of 18 purely on fabric: 3,318 on a full NVLink domain versus 184 on a point-to-point link. THAT is the argument for NVSwitch, expressed as a number. Absolute cost, which is what most people actually want: 4*B*d bytes per rank per layer x 32 layers per token. At B = 1 on a full 450 GB/s per-GPU NVLink path that is 0.0012 ms/token - negligible. At B = 32 it is 0.037 ms; at B = 256, 0.298 ms. On a single 25 GB/s link it is 0.021 ms at B = 1, 0.671 ms at B = 32, and 5.37 ms at B = 256 - at which point the communication is a large fraction of the step. On PCIe 4.0 x16 the numbers are 0.017 / 0.533 / 4.26 ms at B = 1 / 32 / 256. The sensitivity is to B AND to fabric bandwidth multiplicatively, which is why TP over PCIe fails at scale while TP over NVSwitch is invisible.
scales_with: batch_size B (payload is 4*B*d bytes per rank per layer - the cost is LINEAR in B while the weight read it competes with is constant, which is exactly why TP gets harder as you batch more)
interconnect_bandwidth_per_rank (the dominant multiplier: B* ranges from 184 on a single 25 GB/s NVLink 4 link to 3,318 on a full 450 GB/s per-GPU domain - an 18x spread on identical hardware)
tensor_parallel_degree N (ring volume 2*(N-1)/N saturates near 4*s for N >= 4, so cost per rank is roughly flat in N; the win is that P is divided by N)
num_layers (2 communication ops per layer, so the total is linear in depth: 32 layers for a 7B-class model)
hidden_width d (payload is linear in d: 4096 for a 7B, 8192 for a 70B, so the same B* crossover but double the absolute bytes at 70B)
topology (NVSwitch non-blocking vs point-to-point: NVIDIA reports up to 1.5x higher throughput for Llama 3.1 70B on H200 with NVSwitch, which is the same effect as raising BW_link)

whether the layer is row-parallel or column-parallel (only row-parallel layers need the all-reduce; column-parallel needs an all-gather of t tokens instead, whose payload is t*d rather than B*d - and in PREFILL t >> B, which inverts the comparison)

flop_classes.name: TileLang / TileKernels: a tile DSL as the middle layer between hand-written CUDA and Triton
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: The point of a tile DSL is that the author writes tiles and the compiler decides the instruction selection, register/shared-memory allocation and async-copy pipelining. That means the same source can target NVIDIA SM90/SM100 and Huawei Ascend 950 with identical Python APIs, selected automatically at runtime - a portability claim no hand-written CUDA kernel can make. What it costs is the hardware ceiling: a DSL cannot emit an instruction the abstraction does not model, so the fastest path is still whatever the DSL exposes (here: FP8/FP4 block-scaled casts, fused SwiGLU+quant, MoE top-k routing and scoring, RoPE, fused RMSNorm in the Engram gate). Recorded as custom_kernel with class custom_kernel because the mechanism of interest is the compilation layer, not any single op.
scales_with: hardware backend (SM90 / SM100 / Ascend 950)
op (routing, quantization, norm fusion)
precision (FP8 and FP4 casts)

flop_classes.name: TMA (cp.async.bulk.tensor): hardware address generation and predication for global->shared copies
flop_classes.arithmetic_intensity: TMA reduces register pressure and address-computation work in the copy path, which is what allows larger tiles and therefore more FLOPs per byte moved from HBM. The mechanism from the PTX ISA: cp.async.bulk.tensor is a non-blocking instruction that initiates an asynchronous copy of tensor data from .src to .dst, with completion tracked either by an mbarrier (mbarrier::complete_tx::bytes) or by a bulk-group. It is the instruction that makes a tensor map (a host- or device-built descriptor of strides and extents) the unit of transfer, so the hardware does index math and bounds predication. That register saving is the quantitative claim: freed registers mean larger tiles, and larger tiles amortize each HBM byte over more MACs. Three hard scoping facts from the ISA: (1) the .shared::cluster.global direction 'is optimized for' sm_90a/sm_100a/sm_100f/sm_103a/sm_103f/sm_107a/sm_107f/sm_110a/sm_110f and 'may have substantially reduced performance on other targets' - so a cluster-scoped TMA copy on a non-Hopper-plus part is a trap; (2) sub-byte types are NOT supported for .shared::cluster.global on sm_120a, which constrains a cluster-mapped FP4 pipeline on consumer Blackwell; (3) tcgen05.commit gained a .multicast::cluster::32b qualifier and mbarrier.expect_tx gained the same, i.e. multicast completion is a 5th-gen feature. cp.async.bulk.prefetch additionally has a .level::eviction_priority qualifier and applypriority.async.bulk lets the kernel hint L2 eviction policy - the same idea Marlin uses with its immediate-eviction cache policy.
scales_with: architecture generation
tile size enabled by the freed registers
copy direction (global.shared::cta vs shared::cluster.global)
data element size (sub-byte types restricted on sm_120a)
